abstract: |
  Declining body size is widely hypothesized as a general endotherm response to climate warming, but multi-decadal tropical investigations are scarce and reported responses are heterogeneous. Here, we analysed 24 years (1995–2018) of morphology from 73 passerine species (12,571 live-capture records; ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS) across the Brazilian Atlantic Forest under 0.25°C/decade of regional warming. We found little evidence of directional change in body mass (−0.91%/decade, 95% CI: −2.72 to +0.94%) or bill width (−0.03 mm/decade, 95% CI: −0.18 to +0.13), the latter giving no support for Allen-type appendage enlargement. The wing-length trajectory was weakly negative with an interval overlapping zero (−0.74 mm/decade, 95% CI: −1.55 to +0.07), and responses were heterogeneous: 61 of 72 species had intervals spanning zero. On 7,577 records from individuals measured for both traits, body mass was more conserved than cubic geometric shrinkage predicts (+4.85%/decade contrast, 95% CI: +0.81 to +8.89%), rejecting strict geometric isometry: mass and wing length changed independently. Yet, this pattern was unrelated to interannual temperature anomalies. Atlantic Forest passerines therefore show only subtle, species-specific change, and do not reproduce the pronounced responses reported from the central Amazon.
summary-statement: |
  Two decades of warming produced only subtle, species-specific morphological change in Atlantic Forest birds, unlike the pronounced responses reported from the central Amazon.
plain-language-summary: |
  As global temperatures rise, many animals are suspected to be shrinking in body size or changing shape to cope with heat. While birds in the intact Amazon rainforest were recently found to be losing weight and growing longer wings over the past four decades, whether birds in other tropical forests respond similarly has been unclear. Examining 24 years of field data (1995–2018) on 73 songbird species across the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, we find no clear evidence that body mass has changed, while wing length shows subtle, species-specific adjustments rather than uniform shrinking. Bills show no sign of enlargement, and body mass was conserved rather than falling in step with the small changes in wing length. Atlantic Forest birds therefore appear to have changed little in size despite significant regional warming, in contrast to patterns reported from the Amazon. By carefully accounting for differences among the research groups that collected the data, and among field sites and seasons, our study offers a macroecological picture of bird responses to climate change in a fragmented tropical landscape.

```{r load-estimates, include=FALSE}
# format a count with a thousands separator for inline use
.n <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
# format a signed estimate / CI bound to 2 dp with a true minus sign
.s <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))
# format a signed value to 1 dp with a true minus sign
.s1 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", x))
# format a signed estimate to 4 dp with a true minus sign
.s4 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.4f", x))
# format a p-value for inline use
.rp <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste("=", sprintf("%.3f", p))

# pull row from cw_phylo$before_after with optional term filtering
.cw <- function(mod, term = NULL) {
  r <- cw_phylo$before_after[cw_phylo$before_after$model == mod, ]
  if (!is.null(term)) r <- r[r$term == term, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(list(b = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA", dec = "NA", dec_lo = "NA", dec_hi = "NA", n = "NA"))
  list(
    b      = .s(r$estimate[1]),
    lo     = .s(r$ci_lo[1]),
    hi     = .s(r$ci_hi[1]),
    dec    = .s1(r$mm_per_decade[1]),
    dec_lo = .s1(r$mm_per_decade_lo[1]),
    dec_hi = .s1(r$mm_per_decade_hi[1]),
    n      = .n(r$N[1])
  )
}

# multi-trait comparisons from multi_phylo
.mt_phylo <- function(trait_name, mod, term = "scaled_yr") {
  df <- multi_phylo$comparison_lme4
  r <- df[df$trait == trait_name & df$model == mod & df$term == term, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(list(b = "NA", b2 = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA", lo2 = "NA", hi2 = "NA", pct = "NA", pct_lo = "NA", pct_hi = "NA", n = "NA"))
  list(
    b      = .s4(r$phylo_estimate[1]),
    b2     = .s(r$phylo_estimate[1]),
    lo     = .s4(r$phylo_lower[1]),
    hi     = .s4(r$phylo_upper[1]),
    lo2    = .s(r$phylo_lower[1]),
    hi2    = .s(r$phylo_upper[1]),
    pct    = .s1(r$phylo_pct_per_decade[1]),
    pct_lo = .s1(r$phylo_pct_lower[1]),
    pct_hi = .s1(r$phylo_pct_upper[1]),
    n      = .n(r$phylo_n[1])
  )
}

multi_lme4 <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/multitrait_results.rds")
.mt_lme4 <- function(trait_name, mod, term = "scaled_yr") {
  df <- multi_lme4$table
  r <- df[df$trait == trait_name & df$model == mod & df$term == term, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(list(b = "NA", b2 = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA", lo2 = "NA", hi2 = "NA", pct = "NA", pct_lo = "NA", pct_hi = "NA", n = "NA"))
  list(
    b      = .s4(r$estimate[1]),
    b2     = .s(r$estimate[1]),
    lo     = .s4(r$lower[1]),
    hi     = .s4(r$upper[1]),
    lo2    = .s(r$lower[1]),
    hi2    = .s(r$upper[1]),
    pct    = .s1(r$pct_per_decade[1]),
    pct_lo = .s1(r$pct_per_decade_lower[1]),
    pct_hi = .s1(r$pct_per_decade_upper[1]),
    n      = .n(r$n[1])
  )
}

# ---- Bayesian (Stan) tier: the source of every model estimate in the text ----
# bayes_summary.rds from bayes_aggregate.R (posterior pooled over 20 trees);
# bayes_derived.rds from bayes_derived.R (species slopes, diet percentiles).
bayes <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/bayes/bayes_summary.rds")
bder  <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/bayes/bayes_derived.rds")
DEC   <- bder$dec                      # SD-of-year units per decade
.p2   <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
# signed formatters with a true minus sign and an explicit plus
.ss1 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%+.1f", x)); .ss <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%+.2f", x))
.ss4 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%+.4f", x))
# one coefficient of one fit; scale = "mm" (per-decade on the response scale),
# "pct" (log response: % per decade), "sigma" (log residual SD: % per decade),
# "raw" (per unit of the covariate, e.g. per degree C of anomaly)
.bz <- function(fit, par, scale = c("mm", "mm2", "pct", "sigma", "raw")) {
  scale <- match.arg(scale)
  r <- bayes$fixed[bayes$fixed$fit == fit & bayes$fixed$par == par, ]
  na <- list(b = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA", P = "NA", Ppos = "NA", n = "NA")
  if (nrow(r) != 1) return(na)
  f <- switch(scale, mm = function(x) .ss1(x * DEC), mm2 = function(x) .ss(x * DEC), pct = function(x) .ss1(100 * (exp(x * DEC) - 1)),
              sigma = function(x) .ss1(100 * (exp(x * DEC) - 1)), raw = function(x) .ss4(x))
  n <- bayes$meta$n[bayes$meta$fit == fit]
  list(b = f(r$estimate), lo = f(r$lower), hi = f(r$upper), P = .p2(r$p_neg), Ppos = .p2(1 - r$p_neg),
       n = .n(n), est = r$estimate)
}
# sampler diagnostics and agreement with REML, over the fits quoted in the text
local({
  d <- bayes$diag; cm <- bayes$comparison[!grepl("__pcor$", bayes$comparison$fit) &
    grepl("scaled_yr|dT|yr_within|yr_src|yr_mean|:", bayes$comparison$par), ]
  bz <<- list(n_fits = nrow(bayes$meta), rhat_max = sprintf("%.3f", max(d$rhat_max)),
              ess_min = .n(round(min(d$ess_bulk_min))),
              shift_max = sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(cm$diff_in_sd))),
              sd_ratio_max = sprintf("%.2f", max(cm$sd_ratio)))
})

# diet: year x invertebrate share (mm per SD year per SD diet), category contrast, percentile slopes
.bzraw2 <- function(fit, par) { x <- .bz(fit, par, "raw"); if (x$b == "NA") return(x)
  r <- bayes$fixed[bayes$fixed$fit == fit & bayes$fixed$par == par, ]
  modifyList(x, list(b = .ss(r$estimate), lo = .ss(r$lower), hi = .ss(r$upper))) }

n_iso_spp <- sum(bayes$species_slope_dev$fit == .fid[["iso_f"]])
# random-effect SDs (mm) of the fully adjusted wing model, posterior means
.vc <- function(par) .s(bayes$varcomp$estimate[bayes$varcomp$fit == .fid[["w3"]] & bayes$varcomp$par == par])
cw_sd_src <- .vc("sd_src"); cw_sd_site <- .vc("sd_site")

# posterior summary of a variance-component parameter, e.g. h2_slope
.vcz <- function(fit, par) { r <- bayes$varcomp[bayes$varcomp$fit == fit & bayes$varcomp$par == par, ]
  if (nrow(r) != 1) return(list(b = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA"))
  m2 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))
  list(b = m2(r$estimate), lo = m2(r$lower), hi = m2(r$upper)) }
h2s_w <- .vcz(.fid[["w3pcor"]], "h2_slope"); h2s_i <- .vcz(.fid[["iso_fpcor"]], "h2_slope")
cor_w <- .vcz(.fid[["w3pcor"]], "cor_phylo_int_slope")
# REML likelihood-ratio test for a phylogenetic slope component (atlantic_phylo_slopes.R, wing fully adjusted)
.lrt <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/phylo_slopes/phylo_slopes_results.rds")$wing_M3$lrt
lrt_w <- list(sig = sum(.lrt$p_boundary < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), n = sum(is.finite(.lrt$p_boundary)),
              p_med = sprintf("%.2f", median(.lrt$p_boundary, na.rm = TRUE)))
# lagged anomalies, REML across 50 trees (referee_anomaly_lag.R)
lag <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/referee_reruns/anomaly_lag.rds")
.lg <- function(tbl, response, term, dp = 4) { r <- lag[[tbl]]; r <- r[r$response == response & r$term == term, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1); fm <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf(paste0("%+.", dp, "f"), x))
  list(b = fm(r$estimate), lo = fm(r$lower), hi = fm(r$upper), p = .rp(r$p)) }
lg1_i <- .lg("L1", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL", "dT_lag1"); lg12_i <- .lg("L12", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL", "dT_lag12")
lg1_w <- .lg("L1", "wing length (mm)", "dT_lag1", 2); lg12_w <- .lg("L12", "wing length (mm)", "dT_lag12", 2)
lg1_m <- .lg("L1", "log body mass", "dT_lag1"); lg12_m <- .lg("L12", "log body mass", "dT_lag12")

rr          <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/referee_reruns/referee_reruns.rds")

# accessors for the referee re-run tables (Analysis/scripts/referee_reruns.R).
# Every number quoted from these blocks is pulled from the saved object, never
# typed into the text.
.rr_row <- function(tbl, ...) {
  f <- list(...); keep <- rep(TRUE, nrow(tbl))
  for (nm in names(f)) keep <- keep & tbl[[nm]] == f[[nm]]
  r <- tbl[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1L)
  r
}
# thermal-anomaly effects (E1-E3)
rr_therm <- function(model, response, term = "dT", tbl = NULL) {
  tb <- if (is.null(tbl)) rr$E3 else tbl
  r <- .rr_row(tb, model = model, response = response, term = term)
  list(z = .s(r$z), p = .rp(r$p), b = .s4(r$estimate), se = sprintf("%.4f", r$se),
       lo = .s4(r$lower), hi = .s4(r$upper), trees = r$trees_used)
}
# isometry under the M3 adjustment set (E4)
rr_iso <- function(model) {
  r <- .rr_row(rr$E4, model = model, response = "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL")
  list(pct = .s1(r$pct_decade), lo = .s1(r$pct_decade_lo), hi = .s1(r$pct_decade_hi),
       z = .s(r$z), p = .rp(r$p))
}
# thermal-anomaly rows quoted in the Results
rr_iso_therm     <- rr_therm("E3_M3_adjusted_phylo",  "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL")
rr_wing_therm    <- rr_therm("E3_M3_adjusted_phylo",  "wing length (mm)")
rr_mass_therm    <- rr_therm("E3_M3_adjusted_phylo",  "log body mass")
rr_iso_therm_e1  <- rr_therm("E1a_anomaly_plus_year", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL", tbl = rr$E1)
rr_iso_therm_e1b <- rr_therm("E1b_detrended_anomaly", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL",
                             term = "dT_detr", tbl = rr$E1)
rr_iso_therm_e2  <- rr_therm("E2a_locyear_random_intercept", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL",
                             tbl = rr$E2)
rr_iso_yr        <- rr_therm("E1a_anomaly_plus_year", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL",
                             term = "scaled_yr", tbl = rr$E1)
# isometry contrast under the full M3 adjustment set (E4)
rr_iso_m3        <- rr_iso("E4b_iso_M3")
# sample sizes for the thermal models, taken from the fitted tables / data
rr_n_therm  <- unique(rr$E1$n)[1]
# Counted from passer90.rda (ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS only). The same count comes
# from passer90_climate.rds, but that file carries WorldClim-derived columns
# whose terms forbid redistribution, and no climate column is needed here.
rr_n_shared <- local({
  e <- new.env(); load("../Analysis/data/derived/passer90.rda", envir = e)
  nrow(subset(e$passer90, !is.na(conc.wing.length) & !is.na(ln_body_mass)))
})
```

# Introduction

Climate warming can alter animal morphology through several pathways: direct thermoregulatory selection, changes in resource availability, and developmental or evolutionary responses to a shifting environment [@gardner_declining_2011; @sheridan_shrinking_2011; @teplitsky_climate_2014]. These mechanisms have generated prominent predictions, most familiarly that endotherms should become smaller in warmer environments, because a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio aids metabolic heat dissipation [Bergmann's rule; @bergmann1847; @mayr1956; @ashton2002a], and that heat-dissipating extremities such as bills should enlarge [Allen's rule; @allen1877; @ryding2021shape]. Empirical support for such general responses is, however, mixed. Broad syntheses indicate that morphological responses to contemporary warming vary substantially among traits, species, and ecological contexts rather than following a single directional pattern. @radchuk2019adaptive, synthesising phenotypic responses across wild populations, recovered no consistent systematic morphological response to warming. Understanding this heterogeneity requires determining whether the patterns documented in well-studied systems extend to ecological and geographic settings that remain poorly represented in long-term datasets.

Multi-decadal morphological analyses have predominantly drawn on temperate, often migratory, bird species sampled through museum collections or long-term ringing stations in the Northern Hemisphere [e.g., @weeks2020]. Tropical communities, where avian diversity peaks, are far less represented, so it remains unclear how general the reported patterns are. Against this background, @jirinec2021morphological provides a valuable tropical investigation: analysing four decades (1979–2019) of standardised field measurements from 77 non-migratory understorey species in the continuous primary rainforest of the central Amazon (Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project, BDFFP), they documented widespread declines in body mass alongside wing elongation in roughly a third of species, and interpreted the resulting reduction in wing loading as an adaptive shift towards flight economy in an increasingly warm understorey. Whether that pronounced Amazonian response is representative of tropical forest birds more broadly, or is instead strongly context dependent, is the question we address here.

The Brazilian Atlantic Forest offers an informative contrast. It is a global biodiversity hotspot that differs from the continuous lowland central Amazon in almost every respect that might matter: it spans steep topographic and latitudinal gradients, and it has lost over 80% of its original forest cover, leaving the remainder divided among thousands of small, isolated fragments [@ribeiro2009atlantic]. It is therefore a useful test of whether the Amazonian pattern generalises to a tropical forest system with a very different landscape and thermal structure.

Two additional axes may help characterise whatever response is present. First, warming may act on phenotypic variance as well as on trait means, either widening among-individual variation through developmental instability or relaxed selection, or narrowing it through directional canalisation [@teplitsky_climate_2014; @debat2001mapping; @badyaev2005stress]. Second, if morphological change is driven indirectly through food supply rather than directly through thermoregulation [@schmidt_concomitant_2005; @teplitsky_bergmanns_2008], species that depend most heavily on invertebrates should be the most sensitive, and dietary specialisation should help explain variation among species in their trajectories.

Here, we use 24 years (1995–2018) of morphological data from 73 passerine species (`r .n(desc$n_rec)` live-capture records; ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS; @fig-map) to ask whether Atlantic Forest passerines show consistent morphological change across a period of regional warming. We characterise that response in three focal traits—body mass, wing length, and bill width—and then ask how it is structured: whether mass and wing length change in concert on the same individuals or depart from geometric isometry, whether morphology covaries with interannual temperature anomalies, whether among-individual phenotypic variability has changed, and whether dietary reliance on invertebrates explains variation among species.

# Results

## Regional warming across the sampling domain

The analytical dataset comprised `r desc$n_spp` passerine species and `r .n(desc$n_rec)` adult live-capture records (`r .n(desc$n_rec_wing)` wing records across 72 species; *Herpsilochmus pectoralis* has no wing measurements in the compilation and enters only the analyses of the other traits), gathered between 1995 and 2018 across 357 localities spanning the latitudinal and elevational range of the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, from sea level to over 1,500 m (@fig-map). Filtering criteria are given in the Methods.

![Geographic distribution and multi-decadal sampling of `r desc$n_spp` passerine bird species across the Brazilian Atlantic Forest domain. Sampling localities are displayed separately for the early (1995–2006; $n = 2,370$ wing records, 93 coordinate sites, 12 contributors) and late (2013–2018; $n = 2,870$ wing records, 146 coordinate sites, 33 contributors) sampling periods across the biome. Points represent sampling localities coloured by mean wing length, illustrating the broad latitudinal and elevational range covered by the dataset.](images/fig-map.png){#fig-map}

Historical climate data extracted at the 357 capture localities (CRU-TS 4.09 / WorldClim 2.1) documented significant regional warming over the study period: mean annual temperature rose by +0.246°C/decade (95% CI: +0.076 to +0.415°C/decade), representing an average warming of +0.57°C across capture sites between 1995 and 2018. In contrast, precipitation (−44.7 mm/decade, 95% CI: −123.1 to +33.7 mm) and drought indices (SPEI-12: −0.256, 95% CI: −0.617 to +0.105) exhibited no significant directional trends.

These records were contributed by 42 research programmes working in 139 named municipalities, and both the set of active programmes and the geographic focus of sampling shifted substantially over the 24 years (Supplementary Fig. S1, S2). All analyses below therefore incorporate mixed-effects controls for contributor identity, spatial coordinates, elevation, season, moult status, and individual bird identity; the full control ladder, fitted by REML as a check on the Bayesian estimates, is reported in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2.

## Wing length declines weakly, with strong heterogeneity among species

Model-free comparisons of per-species mean trait values between the early (1995–2006) and late (2013–2018) sampling periods showed substantial variation across species (@fig-trends): wing length decreased in 43 species and increased in 18 (@fig-trends A), body mass decreased in 36 and increased in 26 (@fig-trends B), and bill width decreased in 13 and increased in 31 (@fig-trends C).

![Species-level trajectories of wing length, body mass, and bill width between early and late sampling periods. Paired per-species means between the early (1995–2006) and late (2013–2018) periods for (A) wing length ($n = 61$ species), (B) body mass ($n = 62$ species), and (C) bill width ($n = 44$ species) across Atlantic Forest passerines. Lines connect period means for each species, coloured by direction of shift (red = decrease, blue = increase), illustrating the raw interspecific variation across the assemblage.](images/fig-trends.png){#fig-trends}

Unadjusted models suggested a relatively steep decline in wing length over time (baseline model: `r b_w0$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_w0$lo` to `r b_w0$hi`; `r b_w0_pct`%/decade; $P(\beta < 0) = `r b_w0$P`$), but the estimated trend weakened substantially after accounting for contributor identity and the other sources of sampling turnover. In the fully adjusted model, the assemblage-level trajectory was modest and its credible interval overlapped zero: `r b_w3$b` mm/decade (95% CrI: `r b_w3$lo` to `r b_w3$hi`; `r b_w3_pct`%/decade; $P(\beta < 0) = `r b_w3$P`$; @fig-wingtrend). The same model on complete cases gave a similar estimate (`r b_w3cc$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_w3cc$lo` to `r b_w3cc$hi`). Allowing the species year slopes to covary phylogenetically with the species intercepts gave a similar point estimate with a much wider interval (`r b_w3pcor$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_w3pcor$lo` to `r b_w3pcor$hi`; $P(\beta < 0) = `r b_w3pcor$P`$). In that model the phylogenetic share of among-species variance in the year slopes was poorly constrained ($h^2 = `r h2s_w$b`$, 95% CrI: `r h2s_w$lo` to `r h2s_w$hi`), as was its correlation with the intercepts (`r cor_w$b`, 95% CrI: `r cor_w$lo` to `r cor_w$hi`), and a REML likelihood-ratio test found no support for adding a phylogenetic slope component (`r lrt_w$sig` of `r lrt_w$n` trees at $p < 0.05$; median $p = `r lrt_w$p_med`$). The data therefore do not tell us how much of the variation in species' responses follows phylogeny. Separating the year effect within and between contributors showed that the decline was carried mostly by differences among contributors: birds measured by the same contributor changed little over time (`r b_w5in$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_w5in$lo` to `r b_w5in$hi`; $P(\beta < 0) = `r b_w5in$P`$), whereas contributors whose records were later on average recorded shorter wings (`r b_w5btw$b` mm per decade of contributor mean year, 95% CrI: `r b_w5btw$lo` to `r b_w5btw$hi`; $P(\beta < 0) = `r b_w5btw$P`$). Much of the apparent decline in the raw data was therefore associated with changes in sampling structure rather than with a strong assemblage-wide temporal shift. REML estimates for every control tier, and for the first-capture and anomalous-block sensitivity models, are given in Supplementary Table S1; all fall within the same modest range.

![Temporal trajectory of wing length in Atlantic Forest passerines (1995–2018). (A) Within-species-centred wing length over time across 8,478 records from 73 species, with annual means (points, sized by record count). The steep dashed line represents the baseline model (`r b_w0$b` mm/decade); the solid line represents the fully adjusted model (`r b_w3$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI spanning zero). Inset displays wing records per year. (B) Zoomed view of annual means ($\pm 1.96$ SE) and fitted trajectories on the scale of the effect. Model estimates and intervals are posterior means and 95% credible intervals from the posterior pooled over 20 phylogenetic trees.](images/fig-wingtrend.png){#fig-wingtrend}

Species-specific slopes from the fully adjusted model showed pronounced interspecific heterogeneity (@fig-species-slopes): `r sc$neg_point` of `r sc$n` species with wing measurements had negative posterior means, but `r sc$cri_spans_zero` of `r sc$n` had 95% credible intervals overlapping zero. Only `r sc$cri_neg` species declined with intervals excluding zero, and `r sc$cri_pos` increased. The median species slope was `r sc$median` mm/decade. Overall, wing-length trajectories were weakly negative at the assemblage level but highly heterogeneous among species, with substantial uncertainty around the average trend.

![Interspecific heterogeneity in decadal wing-length trajectories under the fully adjusted model. Forest plot of species-specific slopes (mm/decade) across `r sc$n` passerine species, ordered by rate of change. Horizontal bars show 95% credible intervals; filled circles denote species whose intervals exclude zero (red = negative, blue = positive), while open circles denote species whose intervals span zero ($n = `r sc$cri_spans_zero`$ species). Shaded vertical band and solid blue line indicate the assemblage year slope (`r b_w3$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_w3$lo` to `r b_w3$hi`). Hollow grey circles indicate baseline-model slopes.](images/fig-species-slopes.png){#fig-species-slopes}


## Little evidence of directional change in body mass

In contrast to the widespread body mass declines documented in the central Amazon [@jirinec2021morphological], we found little evidence of directional change in body mass across the 24-year record ($n = `r b_m3$n`$ records). The baseline estimate was already slight (`r b_m0$b`%/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_m0$lo` to `r b_m0$hi`; $P(\beta < 0) = `r b_m0$P`$), and it remained close to zero under full adjustment (`r b_m3$b`%/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_m3$lo` to `r b_m3$hi`; $P(\beta < 0) = `r b_m3$P`$) and within contributors (`r b_mw$b`%/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_mw$lo` to `r b_mw$hi`). Unlike wing length, the body-mass estimate therefore changed little across control tiers (Supplementary Table S2).

Live-captured birds gained mass over the course of the day (`r b_hr$b`% body mass per hour, 95% CrI: `r b_hr$lo` to `r b_hr$hi`%, $n = `r b_hr$n`$), consistent with a normal diurnal feeding rhythm. Controlling for capture hour left the decadal slope flat (`r b_mh1$b`%/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_mh1$lo` to `r b_mh1$hi`).

## Mass tends to be retained relative to wing length

The more informative question is how the two traits changed together. We analysed `r .n(rr_n_therm)` shared capture events in which wing length and body mass were measured on the same individual, across `r n_iso_spp` species. Because wing length is a linear dimension ($L^1$) whereas body mass reflects volume ($M \propto L^3$), an animal shrinking uniformly without changing shape—strict geometric isometry—would lose mass at approximately three times the rate of its linear shrinkage ($\% \Delta M \approx 3 \times \% \Delta L$).

On these shared records, under full adjustment, wing length changed by `r b_lnw$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_lnw$lo` to `r b_lnw$hi`%) and body mass by `r b_lnm$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_lnm$lo` to `r b_lnm$hi`%; @fig-isometry A). Strict isometry would predict a mass change of `r b_iso_exp`%/decade from the wing trend alone. Fitted directly, the isometry contrast ($\ln M - 3 \ln L$) changed by `r b_isof$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_isof$lo` to `r b_isof$hi`%; $P(\beta > 0) = `r b_isof$Ppos`$), and by `r b_isop$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_isop$lo` to `r b_isop$hi`%; $P(\beta > 0) = `r b_isop$Ppos`$) under the parsimonious adjustment set. Both estimates point towards mass being retained relative to the wing, but in both the credible interval includes zero, so the shared-individual data do not exclude strict geometric isometry.

Allowing the species year slopes to covary phylogenetically with the species intercepts left the estimate similar but widened its interval (`r b_isofpcor$b`%/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_isofpcor$lo` to `r b_isofpcor$hi`%), and the phylogenetic share of slope variance was again poorly constrained ($h^2 = `r h2s_i$b`$, 95% CrI: `r h2s_i$lo` to `r h2s_i$hi`).

In bivariate morphospace (@fig-isometry B), the 95% credible ellipse for the Atlantic Forest assemblage sits in the region of stasis and mild mass retention, and excludes the decoupling quadrant reported for the central Amazon [@jirinec2021morphological], where wings lengthened as body mass declined. We note that even a clear departure in this contrast would reject only proportional co-variation between mass and wing length; because wing length is itself a functionally labile trait that can change independently of overall structural size, it would not on its own establish a change in whole-body shape.

![Bivariate temporal allometry and test of geometric isometry on shared individuals. **(A)** Decadal rates of morphological change (% per decade) on `r .n(rr_n_therm)` shared records (`r n_iso_spp` species) with simultaneous wing length and body mass measurements, under full adjustment. Points and horizontal bars indicate posterior means and 95% credible intervals, pooled over 20 phylogenetic trees, for wing length, body mass, the mass change expected under cubic geometric scaling ($M \propto L^3$), and the isometry contrast ($\Delta_{\text{iso}} = \ln M - 3\ln L$, fitted directly). The central Amazonian benchmark from @jirinec2021morphological is shown for comparison. **(B)** Bivariate morphological state space ($\Delta\text{Wing}$ vs. $\Delta\text{Mass}$). The solid black line indicates strict geometric isometry ($y = 3x$), the dotted line indicates equal rates ($y = x$), and shaded zones denote proportional shrinkage (blue) and morphological decoupling/slenderisation (red). The green ellipse denotes the 95% credible ellipse for the Atlantic Forest assemblage, encompassing mass stasis and excluding Amazonian slenderisation. Semi-transparent circles represent species-specific estimates ($n = `r n_iso_spp`$).](images/fig-isometry.png){#fig-isometry}

## Annual temperature anomalies are not associated with the wing–mass relationship

If the wing–mass shift tracks thermal conditions, individuals sampled in warmer-than-usual years should depart further from isometry. We tested this by linking each capture to the local annual temperature anomaly ($\Delta T_{\text{local}}$: the capture-year mean temperature at the record's coordinates, minus that locality's own long-run mean; WorldClim historical monthly weather, CRU-TS 4.09 downscaled).

We found no support for it. Under the fully adjusted set used for the temporal models, the isometry contrast was not associated with the annual anomaly ($\beta = `r b_thi$b`$ per °C, 95% CrI: `r b_thi$lo` to `r b_thi$hi`; $P(\beta > 0) = `r b_thi$Ppos`$), and neither were wing length ($\beta = `r b_thw$b`$ mm per °C, 95% CrI: `r b_thw$lo` to `r b_thw$hi`) or log body mass ($\beta = `r b_thm$b`$ per °C, 95% CrI: `r b_thm$lo` to `r b_thm$hi`). The null result is not an artefact of one specification. The anomaly effect on the isometry contrast remained centred near zero when calendar year and the anomaly were entered together ($\beta = `r b_thiy$b`$, 95% CrI: `r b_thiy$lo` to `r b_thiy$hi`), when the anomaly was detrended ($\beta = `r b_thid$b`$, 95% CrI: `r b_thid$lo` to `r b_thid$hi`), and when a locality-year random intercept was added to reflect the fact that all birds caught at one site in one year share a single anomaly value ($\beta = `r b_thil$b`$, 95% CrI: `r b_thil$lo` to `r b_thil$hi`). Parsimonious REML versions of these checks are tabulated in Supplementary Note S4.

Because the sample comprises adults, thermal conditions during development would affect birds captured one or more years later rather than in the year of capture. We therefore refitted the fully adjusted thermal models with the anomaly of the year before capture (lag 1) and with the mean anomaly of the two preceding years, which approximates the natal window (REML, 50 trees; these lag models were not refitted in the Bayesian tier). Neither lagged anomaly was associated with the isometry contrast (lag 1: $\beta = `r lg1_i$b`$, 95% CI: `r lg1_i$lo` to `r lg1_i$hi`; natal window: $\beta = `r lg12_i$b`$, 95% CI: `r lg12_i$lo` to `r lg12_i$hi`) or with wing length (lag 1: $\beta = `r lg1_w$b`$ mm per °C, 95% CI: `r lg1_w$lo` to `r lg1_w$hi`; natal window: $\beta = `r lg12_w$b`$, 95% CI: `r lg12_w$lo` to `r lg12_w$hi`). For body mass, the lag-1 anomaly was centred near zero ($\beta = `r lg1_m$b`$, 95% CI: `r lg1_m$lo` to `r lg1_m$hi`), and the natal-window estimate was positive but its interval included zero ($\beta = `r lg12_m$b`$, 95% CI: `r lg12_m$lo` to `r lg12_m$hi`, $p `r lg12_m$p`$).

In the model containing both terms, the year slope of the contrast (`r b_thiy_yr$b`%/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_thiy_yr$lo` to `r b_thiy_yr$hi`%) pointed the same way as in the temporal models, while the anomaly slope was centred near zero. We therefore make no claim that interannual thermal variation drives any change in the wing–mass relationship.

## Bill width shows little temporal change

Allen's rule [@allen1877; @ryding2021shape] posits that extremities such as bills enlarge in warm climates to facilitate non-evaporative thermoregulatory heat dissipation. Raw species-level trajectories for bill width displayed both increases and decreases across species (@fig-trends C). In a baseline model without contributor controls, bill width appeared to increase (`r b_bl0$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_bl0$lo` to `r b_bl0$hi`; $P(\beta > 0) = `r b_bl0$Ppos`$, $n = `r b_bl0$n`$), a pattern that at face value would be consistent with Allen-type expectations.

However, when contributor and municipality were accounted for, this apparent increase disappeared (`r b_bl1$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_bl1$lo` to `r b_bl1$hi`). In the fully adjusted model, bill width remained flat: `r b_bl3$b` mm/decade (95% CrI: `r b_bl3$lo` to `r b_bl3$hi`; $n = `r b_bl3$n`$). Temporal change within the same contributor was similarly flat (`r b_blw$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_blw$lo` to `r b_blw$hi`). The apparent baseline increase was therefore not robust to the inclusion of contributor identity; because contributors differ in sampling geography as well as in measurement practice, we cannot separate these explanations. Taken together, these analyses give little evidence of bill-width change of the kind expected under Allen-type thermoregulatory predictions.

## Little evidence of change in among-individual phenotypic variability

Climate warming has been hypothesised to alter phenotypic variance as well as trait means [@teplitsky_climate_2014]. Apparent increases in among-individual variability were, however, sensitive to sampling structure.

We used continuous heteroscedastic models, which estimate temporal change in the residual standard deviation ($\sigma$) from the full continuous time series while adjusting for covariates. In the baseline model, $\sigma$ appeared to increase by `r b_s1$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_s1$lo` to `r b_s1$hi`%; $P(\gamma > 0) = `r b_s1$Ppos`$). Adding contributor and municipality random intercepts to both the mean and the residual-SD models reversed the estimate to `r b_s3$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_s3$lo` to `r b_s3$hi`%), with the interval overlapping zero. Adding local mean annual temperature to the residual-SD model yielded no association between residual variance and thermal conditions (`r b_s7t$b`% per SD of temperature, 95% CrI: `r b_s7t$lo` to `r b_s7t$hi`%).

Evidence for increasing phenotypic variability therefore largely disappears once contributor turnover is accounted for, and residual variance was not clearly associated with annual temperature. Because contributors also differ in localities, protocols, and the field workers they employ, this comparison removes pooling across contributors rather than isolating biological variance from observational heterogeneity more generally.

## Dietary specialisation and morphological change

To test whether dietary reliance on invertebrates buffered or accelerated morphological trajectories, we examined species' diet composition from EltonTraits. In continuous interaction models (@fig-dietinteraction, top panel), the baseline model suggested a positive interaction between year and invertebrate diet proportion ($\beta = `r b_dA0$b`$ mm per SD of year per SD of diet, 95% CrI: `r b_dA0$lo` to `r b_dA0$hi`; $P(\beta > 0) = `r b_dA0$Ppos`$). However, adding contributor and municipality intercepts halved this interaction to $\beta = `r b_dA1$b`$ (95% CrI: `r b_dA1$lo` to `r b_dA1$hi`; $P(\beta > 0) = `r b_dA1$Ppos`$), with the credible interval spanning zero. Comparing invertebrate-dominated with other species (@fig-dietinteraction, bottom panel) gave a similarly uncertain interaction under the same controls ($\beta = `r b_dB1$b`$, 95% CrI: `r b_dB1$lo` to `r b_dB1$hi`).

Under the controlled model, the decadal slope for obligate insectivores (species at the 90th percentile of invertebrate diet) was centred near zero (`r b_p90$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_p90$lo` to `r b_p90$hi`). Dietary reliance on invertebrates therefore did not clearly explain variation in wing-length trajectories: apparent interactions in simpler models weakened substantially after accounting for contributor identity, and estimated temporal slopes for highly insectivorous species overlapped zero. We found little evidence that trophic specialisation systematically modified morphological responses over the study period, but the interaction is estimated with considerable uncertainty and we cannot exclude an effect of moderate size.

![Decadal wing-length change as a function of dietary reliance on invertebrates. (Top) Predicted change in wing length (mm) over time across the 10th (p10, blue), 50th (p50, orange), and 90th (p90, red) species-weighted percentiles of invertebrate diet proportion (continuous interaction model), with shaded ribbons denoting 95% credible intervals from the posterior pooled over 20 phylogenetic trees. (Bottom) Predicted wing trajectories for species categorised by primary diet (Invertebrate vs Other). With contributor and municipality intercepts, the interaction attenuates and obligate insectivores exhibit slopes overlapping zero.](images/diet_interaction_plot.png){#fig-dietinteraction}

Whether regional invertebrate availability changed over the same period could not be assessed directly: no standardised, multi-decadal prey monitoring exists for Atlantic Forest understorey.

# Discussion

Do the pronounced morphological responses reported for central Amazonian birds generalise to tropical forest birds more broadly? Across 73 passerine species and 24 years of regional warming in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, our answer is that they largely do not. Morphological change across this regional assemblage was weak, heterogeneous among species, and in several cases not separable from changes in how the dataset was assembled. Ordered as in the Results, we find:
(1) Weak and heterogeneous wing-length change: The average trajectory across species was modestly negative with a credible interval overlapping zero, and `r sc$cri_spans_zero` of `r sc$n` species had credible intervals overlapping zero.
(2) No detectable change in body mass: Unlike in the central Amazon, we found little evidence of directional change, and unlike wing length this estimate was stable across mode specifications.
(3) Mass retained relative to wing length: On shared individuals, body mass tended to be more conserved than cubic geometric shrinkage of the wing predicts, although the credible interval includes strict geometric isometry.
(4) No thermal signal in the wing–mass relationship: The isometry contrast was not associated with annual temperature anomalies under the full adjustment set.
(5) Little evidence of bill-width change: Bill width showed no detectable temporal expansion, giving little evidence of the extremity enlargement expected under Allen-type thermoregulatory predictions.
(6) Little evidence of change in phenotypic variability: Apparent increases in among-individual variability did not survive adjustment for contributor turnover, and residual variance did not track temperature.
(7) No clear dietary modulation: Temporal slopes for highly insectivorous species overlapped zero, giving little evidence that trophic specialisation amplified morphological sensitivity, though the interaction remains uncertain.

## Interspecific variation and the wing–mass relationship

Rather than a uniform response across species, our results reveal substantial interspecific heterogeneity (@fig-species-slopes). While a minority of species exhibited declines in wing length whose credible intervals excluded zero (`r sc$cri_neg` of `r sc$n` species) or comparable increases (`r sc$cri_pos` of `r sc$n` species), the majority (`r sc$cri_spans_zero` species) showed trajectories overlapping zero. This diversity of species trajectories aligns with recent global syntheses showing that morphological responses to climate change are frequently idiosyncratic and species-specific rather than uniform [@teplitsky_climate_2014].

Our analysis of `r .n(rr_n_therm)` shared records from the same individuals suggests that body mass was, if anything, conserved relative to cubic geometric scaling of wing shortening ($P = `r b_isof$Ppos`$ under full adjustment), although strict isometry cannot be excluded. Either way, the data give no sign of the slenderisation documented in the Amazon [@jirinec2021morphological]. Dietary reliance on invertebrates did not clearly explain variation in these trajectories: obligate insectivores exhibited a temporal slope overlapping zero, giving little evidence that trophic specialisation modified morphological responses over this period, though the interaction remains uncertain.

## Contrasting macroecological dynamics: the Atlantic Forest and the central Amazon

These findings present a macroecological contrast to the only comparable multi-decadal Neotropical benchmark: the study by @jirinec2021morphological in the central Amazon. In 77 non-migratory understorey species monitored over 40 years in continuous primary rainforest, @jirinec2021morphological documented widespread declines in body mass coupled with wing elongation in 36% of species. This resulted in a community-wide reduction in wing loading, interpreted as an adaptation to lower metabolic flight costs and improve flight efficiency in an increasingly hot, dry understorey.

The two datasets therefore give different pictures. Before considering why, we note that this is a contrast between two studies rather than a controlled comparison: the Atlantic Forest analysis and the Amazonian study differ not only in landscape context but also in sampling design, temporal coverage, species composition, and measurement structure, and part of the difference may reside in these features. With that caveat, three non-mutually exclusive ecological and evolutionary hypotheses could contribute to a genuine difference. Our data do not discriminate among them, and we present them as hypotheses for future work rather than as conclusions:

First, landscape fragmentation and aerodynamic flight constraints. The central Amazonian study was conducted in a continuous, undisturbed primary forest block (BDFFP) where birds move beneath a continuous closed canopy. In continuous understorey, foraging flights are typically short, highly maneuverable sallies; under such conditions, longer wings and lower wing loading reduce metabolic transport costs with minimal aerodynamic penalty [@jirinec2021morphological]. In contrast, the Atlantic Forest has undergone extensive historical deforestation, leaving a heavily fragmented landscape where forest patches are embedded in open agricultural or pastoral matrices [@ribeiro2009atlantic]. In fragmented landscapes, forest birds must frequently traverse open matrix, cross habitat edges, and navigate areas exposed to strong winds and elevated predation from open-country raptors [@ribeiro2009atlantic]. Under these conditions, aerodynamic performance demands flight power, burst speed, and high maneuverability rather than low wing loading. Selective pressures to navigate fragmented landscapes may therefore penalise wing lengthening or body mass reduction, constraining morphological shifts that might otherwise be favoured in continuous forest.

Second, topographic complexity and elevational thermal refugia. The central Amazon BDFFP site occupies a relatively flat lowland landscape (elevation ~50–150 m) where species have limited access to steep thermal gradients and cannot escape regional warming through short-distance elevational shifts. In contrast, the Atlantic Forest features steep coastal mountain systems (e.g., Serra do Mar, Serra da Mantiqueira) spanning elevations from sea level to over 2,000 m. This complex topography generates sharp microclimatic gradients across short horizontal distances. Birds in topographically complex biomes may buffer themselves against rising temperatures by making subtle elevational or microhabitat shifts, reducing the physiological pressure to undergo morphological adaptation.

Third, microclimatic variability and physiological plasticity. Forest fragments experience pronounced edge effects, with higher temperature variability and fluctuating humidity relative to continuous interior forest. Atlantic Forest birds may already possess high physiological tolerance and plastic buffering capacity to cope with variable microclimates, which would reduce the necessity for directional morphological change over multi-decadal timescales. We emphasise that we did not test this: the diurnal body mass gains recorded here (`r b_hr$b`%/hour) reflect the normal within-day feeding rhythm and are not evidence of thermal plasticity.

Beyond these ecological mechanisms, a plausible alternative hypothesis is whether the contrast reflects study design—namely, a single continuous 40-year ringing station (BDFFP) versus a multi-site macroecological compilation. Our within-contributor Mundlak decomposition makes this less likely as a complete explanation: contributors who sampled birds continuously across multi-year spans (e.g., E. Carrano, A. Ross, M. Alves) independently exhibited slopes indistinguishable from zero (within-contributor wing slope: `r b_w5in$b` mm/decade; complete cases: `r b_w5ccin$b` mm/decade; body mass: `r b_mw$b`%/decade). Restricting the temporal comparison to within a single contributor removes confounding from turnover among research programmes, but it does not remove change over time in the individual field workers, localities, or protocols operating within a programme, so it constrains rather than eliminates a sampling explanation.

## Evaluating ecogeographical rules in tropical endotherms

Our findings provide a critical empirical test of classic ecogeographical rules in tropical endotherms under climate change. Bergmann's rule has frequently been generalised as a general expectation that warming temperatures drive reductions in animal body size [@gardner_declining_2011; @sheridan_shrinking_2011]. In our 24-year dataset of 73 tropical passerine species, we found little evidence of directional change in body mass despite +0.25°C/decade of regional warming. This challenges the generality of Bergmann's rule in tropical forest birds, and indicates that tropical endotherms need not show detectable body-mass loss over decadal timescales.

Similarly, Allen's rule posits that appendages enlarge in warmer environments to facilitate heat dissipation [@allen1877; @ryding2021shape]. While unadjusted baseline models suggested a temporal increase in bill width, this apparent trend did not survive the inclusion of contributor identity, leaving little evidence of bill-width change. In tropical passerines, bill morphology is heavily constrained by foraging biomechanics, trophic specialisation, and vocal performance, which may strongly override subtle thermoregulatory selection for larger bills [@teplitsky_climate_2014].

## The inferential foundation for macroecological trait synthesis

Our study highlights the role of proper data dependency controls when analysing multi-decadal compilations in macroecology. Large-scale compilations such as ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS [@rodrigues_atlantic_2019] are indispensable for macroecological and macroevolutionary research, providing taxonomic and geographic scope that single-site studies cannot achieve. However, because compiled databases combine measurements across dozens of independent research teams, sampling localities, protocols, and seasons, apparent multi-decadal trends can be substantially confounded by sampling turnover.

In our dataset, unadjusted baseline models suggested steep declines in wing length, increases in bill width, and expanding trait variability. Under our multi-tiered comparative framework, the estimated wing decline attenuated by approximately `r b_w_atten`%, the apparent bill expansion disappeared, and the apparent variance inflation was no longer supported. Because contributor identity, sampling geography, protocol, and season are not fully separable in a compilation of this kind, we do not attribute this attenuation to any single source; what the comparison establishes is that the unadjusted estimates were substantially influenced by how the dataset was assembled. Adding contributor identity and individual identity as random intercepts, and latitude, longitude, elevation, season, and moult as fixed effects—within Bayesian phylogenetic mixed models across 20 trees—provided the inferential foundation necessary to properly uncover these biological patterns. Rather than invalidating trait compilations, our findings indicate that large-scale compilations can yield robust macroecological insight when sampling structure is modelled explicitly.

## Conclusion

In summary, 24 years of climate warming in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest have not induced the widespread body mass loss or wing elongation observed in the continuous Amazonian understorey. Instead, we found little evidence of directional change in body mass or bill width, a departure from geometric isometry in which mass is retained relative to wing length, and subtle, species-specific adjustments in wing length. These contrasting responses suggest that landscape fragmentation, topographic complexity, and ecological context shape how tropical species respond to anthropogenic climate change, a hypothesis that our study motivates but cannot itself test.

# Materials and Methods {#sec-methods}

## Trait database filtering and analytical sample derivation

We extracted avian morphological measurements from the ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS database [@rodrigues_atlantic_2019], a comprehensive data compilation comprising `r .n(desc$raw_total)` morphometric entries across the Brazilian Atlantic Forest domain, of which passerines represent `r desc$raw_pass_pct`% (`r .n(desc$raw_passerine)` records). To ensure that temporal analyses reflect genuine living phenotypic variation rather than methodological or preservation artefacts, we implemented a rigorous multi-stage filtering protocol.

First, we restricted the dataset strictly to live field captures, excluding museum study skins. Museum preparation induces post-mortem shrinkage in feathers, bill keratin, and skeletal dimensions (typically 1–3% reduction in linear dimensions upon drying; @weeks2020). Because museum specimens in regional collections are heavily concentrated in earlier decades of the 20th century, retaining study skins introduces artificial positive temporal trends. Second, we restricted records to adult individuals (`Age == "Adult"`), excluding juveniles and fledglings whose flight feathers and bills are incompletely developed. Third, we filtered records spatially to sampling localities falling within a 20-km buffer of the Brazilian Atlantic Forest biome boundary (IBGE/MMA official shapefile), eliminating captures situated in adjacent Cerrado or Caatinga enclaves. The 20-km allowance is the tolerance already applied in the ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS compilation itself, and it accommodates coordinate imprecision and the fact that the mapped biome boundary is a generalisation of a gradual ecotone; it is not a biological buffer and no result depends on its exact width. Fourth, we bounded the temporal window to 1995–2018 (24 calendar years), representing the era of active multi-project mist-netting in the biome with consistent capture documentation. We did not filter on migratory status: the compilation does not record it, and we therefore make no claim that the focal species are strictly resident. The sample comprises the passerines captured by Atlantic Forest mist-netting programmes, which may include partial or altitudinal migrants.

Finally, to guarantee robust parameter estimation for species-level random intercepts and random slopes, we restricted the primary analytical sample to species with $\ge 30$ live-capture records and a temporal sampling span of $\ge 5$ years. This yielded an analytical dataset of `r desc$n_spp` passerine species and `r .n(desc$n_rec)` live-capture records (`r .n(desc$n_rec_wing)` wing-length records across 72 species; one species, *Herpsilochmus pectoralis*, was sampled exclusively for bill and tarsus traits and lacked wing and mass records in the compilation). Wing length was coalesced across database columns, prioritising right wing length when specified, followed by left wing length and unspecified wing length (`conc.wing.length`).

## Accounting for contributor turnover and spatial provenance

In large-scale macroecological compilations aggregating data across independent research programmes, two structural factors can confound temporal trends if left unmodeled: contributor turnover and spatial turnover.

### Contributor turnover and research-group random effects

In avian morphometrics, inter-observer measurement error is well-documented to reach 1–3 mm for wing length and 0.5–1 mm for bill dimensions [@weeks2020]. If different field workers apply slightly different caliper tension or wing-flattening techniques, and if the set of active research programmes changes over time, apparent temporal trends in morphology can arise entirely through turnover in who contributed the data.

In the ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS compilation, the field measurer column (`Measurer`) is 100% missing (NA), so the individual who took each measurement cannot be identified. The identity of the principal investigator and research group coordinator (`Main_researcher`) is, however, 100% complete across all analytical records, comprising 42 distinct entries in our wing dataset. **Throughout this paper we refer to this grouping variable as the *contributor*, meaning the research group or project that supplied the record, and we use this single term consistently in place of "observer" or "measurer".** We emphasise that the contributor is a proxy rather than a direct measure of measurement practice: a contributor random effect absorbs whatever is shared among records originating from the same research programme, which includes caliper and wing-flattening conventions, but also field protocols, target habitats, the set of localities worked, and project-specific species composition. Attenuation of a temporal trend after adding this term therefore indicates that the trend was partly carried by differences among research programmes, and does not by itself isolate measurement error from these other, partly inseparable, sources.

An audit revealed high contributor turnover across the 24-year record: only 6 of the 42 contributors sampled birds in both the early (1995–2006) and late (2013–2018) periods, while the late period experienced an influx of 33 active contributors compared to 12 early (Supplementary Fig. S1). To account for baseline differences among research programmes, we incorporated a random intercept for contributor identity (`(1 | Main_researcher)`).

### Spatial provenance and continuous environmental controls

Over the 24-year timeframe, geographical sampling shifted substantially: early captures (1995–2006) were heavily concentrated in the southern Atlantic Forest (mean latitude $-24.8^\circ$), whereas later captures (2013–2018) expanded northwards (mean latitude $-21.9^\circ$) and into higher elevations (median altitude shifting from 175 m to 489 m). Because widespread passerines frequently exhibit ecogeographical clines in body size, geographic turnover across sampling periods can easily mimic temporal phenotypic change.

To account for continuous spatial and elevational variation without discarding records or introducing artificial clustering, models incorporated standardised latitude (`scaled_lat`), standardised longitude (`scaled_long`), and standardised elevation (`scaled_elev`) as continuous covariates.

### Sampling hierarchy: contributor and municipality random effects

Another structural consideration in multi-source macroecological databases is the relationship between research teams and geographic sampling units. Across the 24-year ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS compilation, individual field projects were typically conducted by distinct research groups operating within specific municipal territories, so the two grouping factors are correlated: in our shared analytical sample ($n = 7,577$), 110 of 128 municipalities (85.9%) were sampled by only a single contributor (and across the full body mass dataset, 129 of 150 municipalities, 86.0%, were sampled by a single contributor).

The two factors nonetheless capture distinct sources of variation. The contributor term absorbs what is shared among records from one research programme, including measurement conventions (caliper tension, wing flattening, scale calibration) and field protocols. The municipality term absorbs local differences among the sampled sites and populations, such as habitat, landscape context, and local population composition, that continuous latitude, longitude, and elevation do not capture. The two are partially crossed rather than nested: in the wing dataset, 14% of municipalities were sampled by more than one contributor, and 64% of contributors worked in more than one municipality, which allows their variances to be estimated separately. Both variances were clearly non-zero in the fully adjusted wing model (among-contributor SD = `r cw_sd_src` mm; among-municipality SD = `r cw_sd_site` mm).

Including municipality also matters for the temporal inference. Because sampling expanded northwards and upslope over the study period, municipality identity is strongly associated with capture year (municipality alone accounts for 74% of the variance in capture year in the wing dataset, against 58% for contributor). Without a municipality term, differences among sites sampled early and late in the series can be read as temporal change. We therefore included random intercepts for both contributor (`(1 | Main_researcher)`) and municipality (`(1 | Municipality)`) in every model beyond the baseline, including the thermal-anomaly and isometry models.

## Model sequence and within-between decomposition

To evaluate how dataset structure influences temporal trends, we fitted a ladder of increasingly controlled mixed-effects models. We refer to each model by a descriptive name; the short codes used in the analysis scripts and in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 are given in parentheses.

- **Baseline** (M0): replicating published unadjusted model structures, with sex, calendar year (`scaled_yr`, centred and divided by its standard deviation, SD = 5.02 years), latitude (`scaled_lat`), species-specific random intercepts and year slopes, and phylogenetic covariance among the species intercepts.
- **+ contributor & municipality** (M1): adding random intercepts for contributor identity `(1 | Main_researcher)`, to absorb systematic differences among research programmes, including but not limited to measurement conventions, and for municipality `(1 | Municipality)`, to absorb local differences among sampled sites.
- **+ wing side, longitude & elevation** (M2): adding fixed effects for the protocol proxy (`wing_col`: right wing, left wing, or side unspecified), standardised longitude (`scaled_long`), and standardised elevation (`scaled_elev`).
- **Fully adjusted** (M3): adding fixed effects for seasonal quarter (DJF: Dec–Feb; MAM: Mar–May; JJA: Jun–Aug; SON: Sep–Nov) to account for feather wear across the annual cycle, active primary moult status (`Molt`), and a random intercept for the individual bird `(1 | ID_individual)` (Ring $\times$ Species) to account for repeated captures of banded individuals.
- **Year within vs between contributors** (M5src; Mundlak within-between decomposition): to separate temporal change occurring within a single contributor from compositional turnover across contributors, calendar year was partitioned into the contributor mean capture year ($\bar{Y}_j = \text{yr\_src\_mean}$) and individual capture deviations from that contributor mean ($Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_j = \text{yr\_within\_src}$) [@mundlak1978pooling; @bell2019fixed], on the fully adjusted specification. The within-contributor coefficient $\beta_{\text{within}}$ measures whether birds contributed by the *same* research programme changed over time, and is therefore not driven by turnover in which programmes were active. It does not, however, remove change over time in the individual field workers, localities, or protocols operating within a programme.
- **Robustness and sensitivity models**:
  - **Fully adjusted, complete cases** (M3_cc): the fully adjusted specification on complete cases ($n = 8,282$). The primary sample ($n = 8,478$) does not discard records with incomplete covariates; instead, missingness is encoded explicitly. Records lacking a recorded altitude take a value imputed from other records at the same coordinates, and season and moult carry an explicit `unrecorded` level rather than being dropped. The complete-case model removes the 196 records with an imputed altitude or an unrecorded season, so the contrast between the two isolates the effect of that encoding.
  - **Fully adjusted, first captures only** (M7): restricted to first captures ($n = 7,791$) to exclude any potential bias from recapture histories.
  - **Fully adjusted, anomalous blocks removed** (M3_noanom): re-fitted after excluding six anomalous sampling blocks (193 records). Blocks are contributor $\times$ municipality $\times$ year cells. For each record we took the deviation of its wing length from its own species $\times$ sex mean, averaged those deviations within each cell, and flagged cells with at least 10 records whose mean deviation exceeded 6 mm in absolute value. The 6 mm threshold is roughly 1.5 residual standard deviations of the fully adjusted fit and about 8% of a typical wing; a shift of that size shared across an entire contributor-site-year block is more consistent with a protocol or data-entry change than with phenotypic variation. Two contributors' late blocks sit 9–12 mm below species means and account for most of the within-contributor decline, which is why the screen exists.

## Bayesian phylogenetic mixed models across 20 topologies

Taxonomic reconciliation between the ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS database and the complete, dynamic avian phylogeny of @mctavish2025tree was executed using the four-stage matching cascade of `prepR4pcm` [@nakagawa2026prepr4pcm]: exact binomial matching, punctuation/spacing normalisation, taxonomic synonym resolution via BirdLife International and IOC checklists, and fuzzy string matching. All 73 passerine species were audited and successfully mapped to phylogenetic tip labels with zero unplaced taxa.

To accommodate phylogenetic uncertainty, we drew 20 alternative phylogenetic topologies from the posterior distribution of @mctavish2025tree. For each tree, we computed the phylogenetic correlation matrix $A$ under a Brownian motion model of trait evolution.

All models were Gaussian linear mixed models fitted in a Bayesian framework with a purpose-written Stan program [@carpenter2017stan]. For the fully adjusted wing model, the length $y_i$ of record $i$ is
$$y_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\beta} + a_{s[i]} + b_{s[i]}\, t_i + c_{k[i]} + m_{j[i]} + u_{r[i]} + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2),$$
where $\mathbf{x}_i$ holds the fixed effects (sex, standardised year $t_i$, latitude, longitude, elevation, season, moult and wing side), $a_s$ and $b_s$ are the intercept and year-slope deviations of species $s$, and $c_k$, $m_j$ and $u_r$ are normally distributed random intercepts for contributor $k$, municipality $j$ and individual bird $r$, each with its own standard deviation. The other models differ only in the terms they include. The species intercepts have a phylogenetic and a non-phylogenetic component,
$$\mathbf{a} = \sigma_a \left( \sqrt{h^2}\, \mathbf{L} \mathbf{z}_{\text{phy}} + \sqrt{1 - h^2}\, \mathbf{z}_{\text{sp}} \right), \qquad \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top = A,$$
with $\mathbf{z}_{\text{phy}}, \mathbf{z}_{\text{sp}}$ standard normal and $\mathbf{L}$ the spectral square root of $A$, so that $\mathbf{a}$ has covariance $\sigma_a^2 [h^2 A + (1 - h^2) I]$ and $h^2$ is the phylogenetic share of among-species variance in the intercepts. Species year slopes $b_s$ are modelled as independent among species rather than as a Brownian process. The individual intercepts are integrated out of the likelihood analytically: the records of one bird are jointly normal with covariance $\sigma^2 I + \tau^2 \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$, whose inverse and determinant have closed forms, so the thousands of individual effects are never sampled. Together with sampling the phylogenetic effects in the eigenbasis of $A$ (after the marginalised spectral models developed by S. Ortega), this makes fitting across many trees feasible.

The response was centred and scaled before fitting and all estimates were back-transformed to the original scale. Priors were weakly informative on that standardised scale: $\mathcal{N}(0, 5)$ for fixed effects, half-Student-$t(3, 0, 1)$ for all standard deviations, $\text{Beta}(1, 1)$ for $h^2$, and $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ for the coefficients of the residual-SD model (below). Each model was sampled separately on each tree with CmdStan 2.39.0 through `cmdstanr` 0.9.0: four chains of 1,000 warm-up and 500 sampling iterations (2,000 warm-up and 2,000 sampling iterations for bill width), with `adapt_delta` = 0.95 and a maximum tree depth of 12. The posteriors from the 20 trees were combined by pooling their draws, which gives the mixture posterior over trees and so carries phylogenetic uncertainty into every estimate [@nakagawa2019rubin]. Across the `r bz$n_fits` models reported here, the largest rank-normalised $\hat{R}$ on any tree was `r bz$rhat_max`, the smallest bulk effective sample size was `r bz$ess_min`, and no sampler divergences occurred [@vehtari2021rhat].

We report posterior means with 95% equal-tailed credible intervals (CrI) and, for temporal effects, the posterior probability that the effect is negative, $P(\beta < 0)$: the share of posterior draws below zero, which is a direct statement of how probable a decline is given the model and data. Values near 0.5 indicate no evidence for either direction.

As an independent check on the estimation engine, every model except the detrended-anomaly and locality-year checks (see *Interannual temperature anomalies*) was also fitted by restricted maximum likelihood with the `propto` covariance structure of `glmmTMB` v1.1.14 [@williams2025glmmtmb] and pooled across 50 trees with Rubin's rules [@nakagawa2019rubin; @nakagawa2026prepr4pcm]. For the temporal coefficients reported here, posterior means and REML estimates differed by at most `r bz$shift_max` posterior standard deviations, and posterior SDs were 1.00–`r bz$sd_ratio_max` times the REML standard errors, as expected when the uncertainty in the variance components is propagated. The complete REML control ladder is given in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2. As a sensitivity analysis, we refitted the fully adjusted wing model and the isometry model with Brownian species slopes correlated with the species intercepts, a structure that `propto` cannot represent.

## Body mass and bill width modelling and testing Allen's rule

To evaluate whether temporal shifts occurred in body mass and extremity dimensions, we applied the sequential control ladder to log-transformed body mass ($n = 11,077$) and bill width ($n = 3,205$). Bill width is the appendage measure used here because it is the extremity trait with the broadest coverage in the compilation and because bill surface is the principal avian site of non-evaporative heat exchange, which is the dimension Allen-type predictions concern. It is, however, a single and imperfect proxy: tarsus length is recorded for fewer individuals, and we did not analyse bill depth or surface area, so our test addresses one extremity dimension rather than heat-dissipating surface as a whole. The fully adjusted models incorporated sex, latitude, longitude, elevation, season, species-specific random intercepts (with phylogenetic covariance) and year slopes, and random intercepts for contributor, municipality and individual bird identity; moult is not recorded for enough of these records to be included.

To evaluate diurnal feeding rhythms in body mass, we extracted recorded capture time (`Hour`) for the 8,345 mass records with available time stamps. Diurnal mass gain was estimated from a model that is not the fully adjusted specification: `ln_body_mass ~ Sex + scaled_yr + scaled_lat + hour_num + season + (1 + scaled_yr || Binomial) + (1 | Main_researcher) + (1 | Municipality)`, restricted to records with a parseable capture time between 05:00 and 19:00. It omits longitude, elevation, moult and individual identity. The same model without `hour_num`, fitted to the identical sample, provides the comparison used to check that the year slope is unaffected by adding capture hour.

To evaluate Allen's rule [@allen1877; @ryding2021shape], which predicts that extremities enlarge in warmer conditions to facilitate non-evaporative heat dissipation, we tested whether bill width exhibited a positive temporal slope under researcher and spatial controls.

## Direct test of geometric isometry

To evaluate whether body shape changed over time, we analysed records with simultaneous measurements of wing length and body mass on the same individual bird. Under geometric isometry, body mass scales with the cube of linear dimensions ($M \propto L^3$), so a bird shrinking uniformly without changing shape loses mass at about three times the proportional rate of its linear shrinkage ($\% \Delta M \approx 3 \times \% \Delta L$).

We tested departure from isometry by fitting the log-scale contrast $\Delta_{\text{iso}} = \ln M - 3 \ln L$ directly as the response. Its year slope is zero under strict isometry whatever the separate trends of the two traits, and fitting it directly yields its posterior without depending on the covariance between two separately estimated slopes. A positive slope indicates that body mass declined less than cubic scaling of the wing predicts (mass conservation or stoutening); a negative slope indicates disproportionate mass loss or wing elongation (slenderisation). The contrast was fitted under two adjustment sets: a parsimonious set (sex, year, latitude, species intercepts with phylogenetic covariance and species year slopes, and random intercepts for contributor and municipality), and the fully adjusted set, which adds longitude, elevation, season, moult and individual identity. To show the two sides of the contrast, $\ln L$ and $\ln M$ were also fitted separately under the fully adjusted set. Year slopes on log scales are expressed as percentage change per decade, $100\,[\exp(10\beta/\text{SD}_{\text{year}}) - 1]$. These models use the `r .n(rr_n_therm)` shared records for which the local temperature anomaly is also available (next section), so that the temporal and thermal tests of isometry rest on identical data.

## Interannual temperature anomalies

Each capture record was linked to the mean annual temperature at its coordinates in its capture year, taken from the WorldClim historical monthly weather series (monthly tmin/tmax, 1950–2024, CRU-TS 4.09 downscaled with WorldClim 2.1, 2.5 arc-min; @harris2020crudata). This is the time-resolved product, not the WorldClim climate normals. The local annual anomaly is that value minus the locality's own mean across the sampled years ($\Delta T_{\text{local}}$). The WorldClim land mask leaves no value at 98 of the 455 coordinate localities, which lie roughly 10 km from the nearest valid cell and are not gap-filled; anomalies were therefore available for `r .n(rr_n_therm)` of the `r .n(rr_n_shared)` shared records.

We tested the association between morphology and $\Delta T_{\text{local}}$ for wing length, log body mass and the isometry contrast ($\Delta_{\text{iso}} = \ln M - 3\ln L$), fitting the fully adjusted set used for the temporal models (sex, latitude, longitude, elevation, season, moult; random intercepts for contributor, municipality and individual; species intercepts with phylogenetic covariance and species anomaly slopes).

Because a temperature anomaly measured over a warming study period is itself correlated with calendar year, and because every bird caught at one locality in one year shares the same anomaly value, we fitted three further specifications of the isometry model, each at the same adjustment level: calendar year and the anomaly entered simultaneously; the anomaly detrended for its linear trend over years; and an additional random intercept for each locality-year. The parsimonious REML versions of these checks are reported in Supplementary Note S4. To allow for delayed effects of conditions during development, the fully adjusted thermal models were also refitted with the anomaly of the year before capture (lag 1) and with the mean anomaly of the two years before capture (lags 1–2, approximating the natal window, since the passerines sampled here typically first breed at about one year old), each expressed relative to the same site baseline. These lag models were fitted by REML in `glmmTMB` across 50 trees only.

## Phenotypic variability: heteroscedastic models

Among-individual phenotypic variability was modelled with continuous heteroscedastic models, which estimate temporal change in the residual standard deviation from the full continuous time series while adjusting for covariates. Alongside the model for the mean, the residual standard deviation $\sigma_i$ of each record had its own log-linear model:
$$\log(\sigma_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 t_i + \gamma_2 \text{Sex}_i \; [+\, f_{k[i]} + g_{j[i]}]$$
where $\gamma_1$ is the change in log residual SD per SD of year, reported as percentage change per decade. In the baseline version the mean model contained sex, year, latitude and the species terms; in the adjusted version both the mean model and the residual-SD model received random intercepts for contributor ($f_k$) and municipality ($g_j$), and the mean model also longitude, elevation and season. A third version added standardised local mean annual temperature (`scaled_tmean`) to the residual-SD model to test whether residual variance tracked thermal conditions.

## Dietary reliance on invertebrates

Species' dietary reliance on invertebrates was extracted from the EltonTraits 1.0 database [@wilman2014eltontraits] (`Diet-Inv`, % of diet consisting of invertebrates). In continuous interaction models, `Diet-Inv` was standardised ($z$-score) and interacted with calendar year (`scaled_yr * diet_inv_std`). Wing-length trajectories were projected across the 10th (p10), 50th (p50), and 90th (p90) species-weighted percentiles of invertebrate reliance. In categorical models, diet was collapsed into Invertebrate-dominated ($\ge 50\%$ invertebrate diet) versus Other (frugivores, nectarivores, granivores, omnivores). Both were fitted as a baseline (sex, latitude, species terms) and with random intercepts for contributor and municipality.

## Use of AI tools

Generative AI tools (Anthropic Claude, accessed through Claude Code) were used
during the analysis and preparation of this manuscript. Their use covered
writing and revising analysis scripts in R, executing those scripts, drafting
and revising manuscript text, and auditing the analysis code for reproducibility.
No AI tool was used to generate, alter or impute data, or to produce figures from
anything other than the analysis outputs described above. All analyses were
re-executed from the archived scripts and all reported values are read
programmatically from the saved model objects rather than transcribed. All
authors have verified the claims that remain.

## Reproducible software environment

The Bayesian models were fitted on a Linux server in R 4.5.3 with CmdStan 2.39.0 through `cmdstanr` (v0.9.0), using the Stan program archived as `Analysis/scripts/stan/phylo_lmm_marginal.stan`. All other analyses and manuscript generation were conducted in R 4.6.0 with `glmmTMB` (v1.1.14), `prepR4pcm` (v0.5.0.9000), `metafor` (v5.0-1), `lme4` (v2.0-1), `ape` (v5.8-1), `phytools` (v2.5-2), `sf` (v1.1-2) and `terra` (v1.9-27), alongside Python (3.11 or later) with `matplotlib` and `pandas` for the figures. The complete environment, giving the exact version and source of every package, is recorded in `renv.lock` at the root of the archived repository and can be restored with `renv::restore()`; `Analysis/output/session_info.txt` gives the same information in human-readable form. Each saved model object additionally records the R and engine version under which it was fitted. All analysis scripts, curated datasets, and fitted model objects are openly archived and fully reproducible in the project repository (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.atlantic_birds).

# Data and resource availability {.unnumbered}

All primary data analysed here are from the previously published, openly
available compilations of morphological records from ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS
[@rodrigues_atlantic_2019]. Climate data are from the WorldClim historical
monthly weather series (CRU-TS 4.09 downscaled; @harris2020crudata). Phylogenies were drawn from the posterior distribution of
@mctavish2025tree. Dietary data are from EltonTraits 1.0 [@wilman2014eltontraits].

Analysis code, the derived analytical datasets, and the fitted model objects
needed to reproduce every value reported here are archived at
